group.name: Cisco OS Receiver
group.description: Dashboard group for Cisco OS receiver metrics in Splunk Observability Cloud. It includes an overview landing page plus focused pages for telemetry health, interfaces, routing/fabric/redundancy, AI/RDMA/QoS congestion, hardware/optics, secure networking, and campus networking troubleshooting.

dashboards.name: 00 Overview Troubleshooting Workflow
dashboards.description: Value: gives ITOps and NetOps a single landing page for Cisco OS receiver metrics, from telemetry trust through interface, routing, fabric, AI/RDMA, QoS, optics, and hardware troubleshooting.
dashboards.value: A high-density operational landing page for live troubleshooting and incident autopsy. It prioritizes chart styles by the question each metric answers: list charts for current state and exceptions, time-series charts for rates, utilization, drops, marks, counts, churn, temperature, and capacity signals.

charts.name: Value Provided
charts.description: Value: explains how to use the overview dashboard as the incident starting point. Interpretation: start here when the failure domain is unknown, then jump to a focused page when the symptom points at a device, interface, routing, redundancy, AI/RDMA, QoS, optics, or hardware issue.
charts.markdown:
## Value Provided
Use this overview dashboard as the first Splunk Observability view during Cisco network incidents and post-incident autopsy. It is intentionally organized as a workflow: prove telemetry is trustworthy, isolate link and interface symptoms, confirm routing/fabric/redundancy state, then inspect AI/RDMA, QoS, optics, and hardware evidence.

Chart style is intentional. Current binary state is shown as list charts with sparklines so failed devices, interfaces, peers, VNIs, and members are easy to spot without reading flat 1/0 lines. Rates, utilization, drops, marks, temperatures, counts, and churn stay as time-series charts because timing and slope are the most useful troubleshooting evidence. Single-value cards are avoided because these metrics are multi-device and multi-interface by nature.

charts.name: 1. Telemetry Trust And Device Health
charts.description: Value: separates the single dashboard into an incident workflow section. Interpretation: use this header to move through related charts together instead of reading every panel as an isolated signal.
charts.markdown:
### 1. Telemetry Trust And Device Health
Start here before trusting downstream network conclusions. Confirm the device is reachable, the scrape is complete, command families are not failing, and device pressure or reloads did not distort the evidence.

charts.name: Device Reachability By Host
charts.description: Value: identifies devices that stopped responding to collection before deeper analysis begins. Interpretation: each row is a device; 1 means reachable and 0 means unreachable. Use the sparkline to spot flapping reachability.

charts.name: Scrape Partial Success
charts.description: Value: prevents false conclusions from incomplete telemetry when only some command families failed. Interpretation: each row is a device; 1 means at least one command family failed during collection. Check command duration and errors next.

charts.name: Command Duration By Family
charts.description: Value: isolates slow command families that explain stale, partial, or missing data. Interpretation: higher values show longer CLI command execution by device and command family; spikes identify the scraper area causing latency.

charts.name: SSH Reconnects And Command Errors
charts.description: Value: separates network/session instability from parser or command-family failures. Interpretation: rising reconnects suggest SSH/session path issues; rising command errors by family suggest unsupported commands, privilege gaps, or device CLI failures.

charts.name: CPU And Memory Pressure
charts.description: Value: finds device resource exhaustion that can precede control-plane instability and packet loss. Interpretation: values are percentages by device; sustained high CPU or memory during an incident points to device pressure rather than only a link issue.

charts.name: Reload Evidence
charts.description: Value: confirms whether a reboot or reload occurred near the outage window. Interpretation: uptime should climb steadily; a sharp drop means the device restarted and should anchor the incident timeline.

charts.name: 2. Interface And Link Symptoms
charts.description: Value: separates the single dashboard into an incident workflow section. Interpretation: use this header to move through related charts together instead of reading every panel as an isolated signal.
charts.markdown:
### 2. Interface And Link Symptoms
Separate intentional shutdown, operational failure, saturation, silence, packet-rate pressure, speed downgrade, errors, and drops on service-carrying links.

charts.name: Admin State Compared To Oper State
charts.description: Value: distinguishes intentionally disabled interfaces from enabled interfaces that failed. Interpretation: Admin enabled=1 means the port should be active; Oper up=0 means the link is down. The important exception is admin 1 with oper 0.

charts.name: Interface Utilization
charts.description: Value: identifies saturated links and asymmetric congestion by direction. Interpretation: values are percent utilization by device, interface, and direction; sustained high utilization before impact suggests capacity pressure.

charts.name: Interface Traffic Rate
charts.description: Value: finds sudden silence, traffic shifts, or burst growth on critical ports. Interpretation: bytes/sec is shown by interface and direction; drops to zero or sudden directional shifts are strong incident markers.

charts.name: Interface Packet Rate
charts.description: Value: differentiates packet-rate pressure from byte-rate saturation. Interpretation: high packets/sec with modest byte/sec can indicate small-packet storms, control traffic, or workload patterns stressing forwarding paths.

charts.name: Interface Errors And Drops
charts.description: Value: highlights packet-loss symptoms that correlate with application latency, retransmits, or failover events. Interpretation: non-zero sustained errors/sec or drops/sec on clean links is actionable; compare timing with utilization and optics.

charts.name: Interface Speed
charts.description: Value: exposes speed downgrade or missing speed data that makes utilization misleading. Interpretation: each row is a current interface speed; unexpected lower speed explains apparent saturation and should be checked against physical/link settings.

charts.name: 3. Routing Fabric And Redundancy
charts.description: Value: separates the single dashboard into an incident workflow section. Interpretation: use this header to move through related charts together instead of reading every panel as an isolated signal.
charts.markdown:
### 3. Routing Fabric And Redundancy
Validate whether control-plane, forwarding-plane, overlay, L2, and redundant path state changed before or during impact.

charts.name: Routing Neighbor State
charts.description: Value: identifies BGP, OSPF, EIGRP, or ISIS adjacencies that dropped or flapped. Interpretation: each row is a neighbor; 1 means established/up and 0 means down or not established. Use the sparkline to see flaps.

charts.name: Route, ARP, Adjacency, And FIB Counts
charts.description: Value: compares routing inventory with forwarding inventory to spot control-plane or forwarding-plane divergence. Interpretation: counts should move coherently; route/FIB divergence or ARP/adjacency collapse narrows root cause.

charts.name: Forwarding And QFP Drops
charts.description: Value: surfaces data-plane drop reasons after route convergence or policy changes. Interpretation: watch rate by reason/source/interface; new or rising rates identify where packets are being discarded.

charts.name: VXLAN NVE And VNI Status
charts.description: Value: shows overlay reachability and tenant segment health on NX-OS fabrics. Interpretation: each row is an NVE peer or VNI; 1 means up and 0 means down. Correlate down rows with EVPN route count changes.

charts.name: EVPN Route Counts
charts.description: Value: detects overlay route churn or tenant route loss. Interpretation: drops by VRF or route type suggest tenant reachability loss; unexpected growth can indicate route leaks or churn.

charts.name: Redundant AI Path Health
charts.description: Value: shows whether port-channel members or vPC peers degraded capacity while the aggregate path still looked available. Interpretation: port-channel and member status should be 1, vPC status should be 1, and consistency failures should be 0; any opposite value can create hot links and AI collective slowdown.

charts.name: LACP Errors And Packets
charts.description: Value: identifies negotiation instability before traffic visibly fails. Interpretation: errors/sec should normally be zero; packet changes without corresponding health can indicate negotiation or peer issues.

charts.name: STP Topology Changes
charts.description: Value: catches topology churn that can reroute or blackhole traffic. Interpretation: bursts of topology changes mark L2 instability; correlate the timing with port-channel, vPC, routing, and interface symptoms.

charts.name: 4. AI RDMA QoS Physical Evidence
charts.description: Value: separates the single dashboard into an incident workflow section. Interpretation: use this header to move through related charts together instead of reading every panel as an isolated signal.
charts.markdown:
### 4. AI RDMA QoS Physical Evidence
For AI, storage, and RDMA/RoCEv2 workloads, correlate congestion feedback, lossless backpressure, queue drops, watchdog intervention, optics drift, thermal pressure, and hardware state.

charts.name: RoCEv2 Congestion Control Loop
charts.description: Value: shows the switch-side RDMA/RoCEv2 control loop from ECN marking to PFC backpressure to drops or PFC watchdog intervention. Interpretation: ECN marks should normally appear before PFC or drops; PFC without ECN can indicate threshold, classification, or microburst issues, while queue drops or watchdog activity mean congestion control failed or a queue became stuck.
charts.signalflow: data('cisco.interface.qos.policy.packets', filter=filter('cisco.qos.action', 'mark')).rate().sum(by=['host.name', 'network.interface.name', 'network.io.direction', 'cisco.qos.class', 'cisco.qos.drop.reason']).publish(label='ECN marks/sec'); data('cisco.interface.pause.frames', filter=filter('cisco.pause.type', 'pfc')).rate().sum(by=['host.name', 'network.interface.name', 'network.io.direction', 'cisco.qos.priority']).publish(label='PFC pause/sec'); data('cisco.interface.qos.queue.packets', filter=filter('cisco.qos.action', 'drop')).rate().sum(by=['host.name', 'network.interface.name', 'network.io.direction', 'cisco.qos.group', 'cisco.qos.drop.reason']).publish(label='Queue drops/sec'); data('cisco.interface.qos.queue.packets', filter=filter('cisco.qos.source', 'pfc_watchdog')).rate().sum(by=['host.name', 'network.interface.name', 'cisco.qos.group', 'cisco.qos.action']).publish(label='PFC watchdog/sec')

charts.name: PFC And Flow-Control Pause Pressure
charts.description: Value: identifies lossless Ethernet backpressure before packet loss is obvious to applications. Interpretation: rising receive pause frames usually means the local interface is asking its peer to slow down; rising transmit pause frames means the peer is congested. Persistent PFC on GPU-facing or spine-facing links is a strong workload-impact signal.

charts.name: ECN And WRED Congestion Feedback
charts.description: Value: shows whether the fabric is signaling congestion to RoCEv2 endpoints before drops occur. Interpretation: ECN mark rates mean congestion feedback is active; WRED or tail-drop rates mean congestion has crossed into loss. Marks without drops can be healthy congestion control, while marks plus drops point to under-sized buffers, hot spots, or traffic imbalance.

charts.name: Lossless Queue Drops And Drains
charts.description: Value: pinpoints the queue, QoS group, direction, and drop reason affecting AI/RDMA traffic. Interpretation: lossless queues should not show sustained packet drops; drain activity implies protection or recovery behavior, and drop activity means loss that can stall RDMA/NCCL-style workloads.

charts.name: Optical Power Drift
charts.description: Value: links GPU path errors or retransmission symptoms to RX/TX optical power drift. Interpretation: falling RX power or rising TX power before errors and pause frames suggests optics, cabling, or environmental root cause rather than workload imbalance.
charts.signalflow: data('cisco.transceiver.sensor', filter=filter('cisco.transceiver.sensor', 'rx_power')).mean(by=['host.name', 'network.interface.name', 'cisco.transceiver.lane']).publish(label='RX optical power dBm'); data('cisco.transceiver.sensor', filter=filter('cisco.transceiver.sensor', 'tx_power')).mean(by=['host.name', 'network.interface.name', 'cisco.transceiver.lane']).publish(label='TX optical power dBm')

charts.name: Hardware Temperature
charts.description: Value: identifies thermal pressure tied to slots, components, or chassis-wide events. Interpretation: rising temperature before errors or reloads suggests physical/environmental cause.

charts.name: Hardware Component Status
charts.description: Value: surfaces fan, PSU, module, chassis, and inventory states that can precede device failure. Interpretation: use the Cisco state label first; numeric values are -1 unknown, 0 critical, 1 ok, and 2 warning.

Interpretation: correlate transport and VPN health with edge datapath utilization, QFP drops, control-plane protection, and protocol errors to decide whether the issue is carrier, tunnel, policy, device pressure, or forwarding.
charts.markdown:
## Value Provided
Use this page for secure networking and branch-edge incidents. It combines Cisco OS edge/router telemetry with Meraki MX signals: WAN uplink state, loss, latency, cellular signal, VPN reachability and quality, appliance performance, QFP datapath utilization, crypto/NAT/QoS/punt/IP drop families, forwarding drops, control-plane protection, punt pressure, and protocol errors.

Read it left to right during triage: prove transport and VPN quality, check edge forwarding pressure, inspect drops by feature or reason, then use control-plane and protocol panels to separate policy/protection behavior from device overload or carrier path degradation.

charts.name: Secure Edge Device And Uplink State
charts.description: Value: shows whether secure edge devices and WAN uplinks are reachable before deeper datapath analysis. Interpretation: Cisco OS device up should be 1, Meraki appliance status should be healthy/online, and active uplinks should remain usable during the incident.
charts.signalflow: data('cisco.device.up').mean(by=['host.name']).publish(label='Cisco OS device up'); data('meraki.device.status', filter=filter('meraki.device.product_type', 'appliance')).mean(by=['host.name', 'host.id', 'meraki.device.status']).publish(label='MX status'); data('meraki.uplink.status').mean(by=['host.name', 'host.id', 'meraki.uplink.interface', 'meraki.uplink.status', 'meraki.uplink.provider']).publish(label='MX uplink active')

charts.name: WAN Loss Latency And VPN Quality
charts.description: Value: correlates carrier path quality with VPN tunnel experience. Interpretation: WAN loss/latency that starts before VPN loss, jitter, or MOS degradation points to transport; VPN degradation without WAN degradation points to tunnel, peer, or policy issues.
charts.signalflow: data('meraki.uplink.loss').mean(by=['host.name', 'host.id', 'meraki.uplink.interface']).publish(label='WAN loss %'); data('meraki.uplink.latency').mean(by=['host.name', 'host.id', 'meraki.uplink.interface']).publish(label='WAN latency ms'); data('meraki.vpn.peer.loss').mean(by=['host.name', 'meraki.vpn.peer.name', 'meraki.vpn.sender.uplink', 'meraki.vpn.receiver.uplink']).publish(label='VPN loss %'); data('meraki.vpn.peer.latency').mean(by=['host.name', 'meraki.vpn.peer.name', 'meraki.vpn.sender.uplink', 'meraki.vpn.receiver.uplink']).publish(label='VPN latency ms'); data('meraki.vpn.peer.jitter').mean(by=['host.name', 'meraki.vpn.peer.name']).publish(label='VPN jitter ms'); data('meraki.vpn.peer.mos').mean(by=['host.name', 'meraki.vpn.peer.name']).publish(label='VPN MOS')

charts.name: VPN Peer Reachability
charts.description: Value: identifies Auto VPN or third-party VPN peers that are unreachable. Interpretation: 1 means reachable; 0 means unreachable. Use peer type/name/network ID to scope the branch or partner tunnel.

charts.name: Edge Datapath Utilization And Traffic
charts.description: Value: shows whether the secure edge datapath is approaching capacity. Interpretation: high QFP load, high packet rate, or falling Meraki appliance score during user impact points to device pressure rather than only carrier quality.

charts.name: Security Path Drops By Feature And Reason
charts.description: Value: reveals crypto, NAT, QoS, punt, IP, and forwarding drop reasons that interface counters alone can miss. Interpretation: drops by source/reason tell whether the secure path is losing traffic because of policy, feature handling, lookup, resource, or datapath behavior.

charts.name: Interface And QFP Drop Locality
charts.description: Value: ties datapath drops back to the interface and direction carrying affected traffic. Interpretation: if QFP interface drops line up with interface errors or packet drops, start at that edge handoff or secure-zone interface.
charts.signalflow: data('cisco.qfp.interface.drops').rate().sum(by=['host.name', 'network.interface.name', 'network.io.direction']).publish(label='QFP interface drops/sec'); data('system.network.errors', filter=filter('hw.type', 'network')).rate().sum(by=['host.name', 'network.interface.name', 'network.io.direction']).publish(label='Interface errors/sec'); data('system.network.packet.dropped', filter=filter('hw.type', 'network')).rate().sum(by=['host.name', 'network.interface.name', 'network.io.direction']).publish(label='Interface drops/sec')

charts.name: Control Plane Protection And Punt Pressure
charts.description: Value: shows whether protection policy or punt traffic is affecting the secure edge. Interpretation: rising control-plane drops can be healthy protection or policy impact; high punt rates mean traffic is leaving hardware forwarding and stressing CPU paths.

charts.name: Protocol Errors And Drops
charts.description: Value: surfaces protocol-level traffic the device is rejecting or failing to process. Interpretation: ICMP, TCP, UDP, routing, or IP error/drop spikes help distinguish malformed traffic, scanning, routing instability, or application path failures.

charts.name: Cellular Backup Signal
charts.description: Value: explains whether backup cellular quality is driving secure edge degradation. Interpretation: worsening RSRP/RSRQ before loss or tunnel degradation points to cellular coverage, antenna, provider, or failover-path issues.

dashboards.name: 07 Campus Networking
dashboards.description: Value: combines Cisco OS switch/L2/physical telemetry with Meraki switching and wireless experience for campus troubleshooting.
dashboards.value: Use this page when the incident involves access switches, APs, SSIDs, clients, PoE, topology, L2 stability, uplinks, or campus physical paths.

charts.name: Value Provided
charts.description: Value: explains the campus networking workflow. Interpretation: combine switch port state, utilization, L2 stability, topology, PoE, Meraki port alerts, AP/client load, RF utilization, SSID state, wireless loss, optics, and power-module signals to move from user symptom to affected access path.
charts.markdown:
## Value Provided
Use this page for campus networking incidents across access switching and wireless. It blends Cisco OS switch telemetry with Meraki switching and wireless signals: port admin/oper state, utilization, byte/packet volume, errors/drops, err-disabled ports, Meraki port alerts, PoE allocation, AP status, client count, channel utilization, wireless packet loss, SSID broadcast status, L2/STP churn, port-channel/LACP/vPC health, topology neighbors, optics, and power modules.

Start with device and access-port state, then check utilization and packet loss. If the issue is wireless, move to AP status, clients, RF utilization, packet loss, and SSID status. If the issue is wired or building-wide, inspect L2 stability, topology, PoE, power, and optics.

charts.name: Campus Device AP And Switch Health
charts.description: Value: shows whether campus switches and APs are reachable before interpreting access symptoms. Interpretation: down Cisco OS devices, offline Meraki switches, or offline APs define the failure domain quickly.
charts.signalflow: data('cisco.device.up').mean(by=['host.name']).publish(label='Cisco OS device up'); data('meraki.device.status', filter=filter('meraki.device.product_type', 'switch')).mean(by=['host.name', 'host.id', 'meraki.device.status']).publish(label='Meraki switch status'); data('meraki.device.status', filter=filter('meraki.device.product_type', 'wireless')).mean(by=['host.name', 'host.id', 'meraki.device.status']).publish(label='AP status')

charts.name: Access Port Admin Versus Oper State
charts.description: Value: separates intentionally disabled ports from failed links across Cisco OS and Meraki switching. Interpretation: admin enabled with oper down needs physical, endpoint, PoE, or access-policy investigation.
charts.signalflow: data('cisco.interface.admin.status').mean(by=['host.name', 'network.interface.name']).publish(label='Cisco admin enabled'); data('system.network.interface.status', filter=filter('hw.type', 'network')).mean(by=['host.name', 'network.interface.name']).publish(label='Cisco oper up'); data('cisco.interface.admin.status', filter=filter('os.name', 'Meraki')).mean(by=['host.name', 'host.id', 'network.interface.name']).publish(label='Meraki admin enabled'); data('system.network.interface.status', filter=filter('os.name', 'Meraki')).mean(by=['host.name', 'host.id', 'network.interface.name']).publish(label='Meraki port up')

charts.name: Campus Utilization Traffic And Packet Rate
charts.description: Value: shows wired campus saturation, sudden silence, and packet-rate pressure. Interpretation: sustained high utilization, high packet rate, or asymmetric traffic can explain user impact even when links stay up.
charts.signalflow: data('cisco.interface.utilization').mean(by=['host.name', 'network.interface.name', 'network.io.direction']).scale(100).publish(label='Cisco utilization %'); data('system.network.io', filter=filter('hw.type', 'network')).rate().sum(by=['host.name', 'network.interface.name', 'network.io.direction']).publish(label='Cisco bytes/sec'); data('cisco.interface.packet.rate').mean(by=['host.name', 'network.interface.name', 'network.io.direction']).publish(label='Cisco packets/sec'); data('cisco.interface.utilization', filter=filter('os.name', 'Meraki')).mean(by=['host.name', 'host.id', 'network.interface.name', 'network.io.direction']).scale(100).publish(label='Meraki utilization %'); data('meraki.switch.port.usage').sum(by=['host.name', 'host.id', 'network.interface.name', 'network.io.direction']).publish(label='Meraki usage KBy')

charts.name: Campus Errors Drops And Port Alerts
charts.description: Value: combines Cisco interface loss symptoms with Meraki Dashboard port alerts. Interpretation: interface errors or drops plus port alerts point to cabling, endpoint, PoE, CRC, or policy issues on a specific access path.
charts.signalflow: data('system.network.errors', filter=filter('hw.type', 'network')).rate().sum(by=['host.name', 'network.interface.name', 'network.io.direction']).publish(label='Cisco errors/sec'); data('system.network.packet.dropped', filter=filter('hw.type', 'network')).rate().sum(by=['host.name', 'network.interface.name', 'network.io.direction']).publish(label='Cisco drops/sec'); data('cisco.interface.errdisabled').mean(by=['host.name', 'network.interface.name', 'cisco.errdisabled.reason']).publish(label='Err-disabled'); data('meraki.switch.port.alert').sum(by=['host.name', 'host.id', 'network.interface.name', 'meraki.switch.port.alert.severity', 'meraki.switch.port.alert.reason']).publish(label='Meraki port alerts')

charts.name: Wireless Clients RF Utilization And Loss
charts.description: Value: correlates AP client load, RF airtime pressure, and packet loss. Interpretation: high client load plus high channel utilization or loss points to RF/load; loss without RF pressure can indicate AP, client, roaming, or upstream path symptoms.

charts.name: SSID Broadcast Status
charts.description: Value: catches SSIDs that are disabled, not advertised, or not broadcasting. Interpretation: 1 means enabled, advertised, and broadcasting; 0 means clients may not discover or join that BSS.

charts.name: Campus L2 Stability And Redundancy
charts.description: Value: shows spanning-tree churn, blocked ports, port-channel health, LACP negotiation, and vPC health. Interpretation: churn, member loss, LACP errors, or vPC inconsistency can create intermittent campus outages while some paths remain up.
charts.signalflow: data('cisco.l2.stp.topology_changes').rate().sum(by=['host.name', 'cisco.l2.vlan', 'network.interface.name']).publish(label='STP changes/sec'); data('cisco.l2.stp.blocked_ports').mean(by=['host.name', 'cisco.l2.vlan', 'network.interface.name']).publish(label='STP blocked ports'); data('cisco.port_channel.member.status').mean(by=['host.name', 'cisco.port_channel.name', 'network.interface.name', 'cisco.port_channel.state']).publish(label='Port-channel member up'); data('cisco.lacp.errors').rate().sum(by=['host.name', 'network.interface.name', 'cisco.lacp.error.type']).publish(label='LACP errors/sec'); data('cisco.vpc.consistency.failures').mean(by=['host.name', 'cisco.vpc.check']).publish(label='vPC consistency failures')

charts.name: Campus Topology Neighbors
charts.description: Value: shows LLDP/CDP neighbor evidence so operators can spot wrong connections or missing neighbors. Interpretation: use local interface, neighbor name, neighbor interface, and protocol to confirm the physical campus path.

charts.name: PoE Power Modules And Physical Access Path
charts.description: Value: ties endpoint power and physical health to campus symptoms. Interpretation: PoE allocation changes, failed power modules, optical drift, or hot optics explain phones, APs, cameras, or uplinks failing without a routing incident.
charts.signalflow: data('meraki.switch.port.poe.allocated').mean(by=['host.name', 'host.id', 'network.interface.name']).publish(label='PoE allocated W'); data('meraki.power.module.status').mean(by=['host.name', 'host.id', 'meraki.power.slot', 'meraki.power.module.status']).publish(label='Power module status'); data('cisco.transceiver.sensor', filter=filter('cisco.transceiver.sensor', 'rx_power')).mean(by=['host.name', 'network.interface.name', 'cisco.transceiver.lane']).publish(label='RX optical power dBm'); data('cisco.transceiver.sensor', filter=filter('cisco.transceiver.sensor', 'temperature')).mean(by=['host.name', 'network.interface.name', 'cisco.transceiver.lane']).publish(label='Optic temperature C')
